blocks.x: This is Ron Warren inviting you to come with me as we enter those swinging doors to Speakeasy Junction where they play that good old Dixieland jazz. We'll be here enjoying some of the finest in Dixieland and traditional jazz from every era of jazz history with special emphasis on the music of the 1920s, the golden era of the music we enjoy. So sit back and relax with your bathtub booze while we listen to some of the finest music ever to be called jazz.

Charleston, Charleston, made in Carolina. Some dance, some dance. I'll say there's nothing finer than the Charleston, Charleston. Boy, how you can shuffle. Every step you do, this is something new. Man, I'm telling you, it's a lot of zoopock dance. Wing dance will be a back number. But the Charleston, the new Charleston, that dance is surely a come. But sometimes you'll dance it one time. The dance called the Charleston, when it's off your line.

We are going to have a special two-hour session of the program this evening, devoted to music from Australia, from the land down under. And we have with us tonight our special guest commentator, Mr. Eric Brown. And he is going to fill us in on some of the details of the music we're going to be listening to from Australia. We'll be getting to our first selection in just a moment. We'd like to welcome to Speakeasy Junction this evening, Mr. Eric Brown, who is going to tell us a little bit about the music we're going to be listening to. But before we get to our first recording, Eric, could you tell us where you are from in Australia, and perhaps maybe a little bit about the music that we're going to hear, some of the clubs that you belong to, and just a little bit about the area itself.

OK, Ron. First of all, I'm not a musician. I'm a record collector. And I come from Melbourne, which is on the southern coast of Australia, and it's Australia's second biggest city with a population of about two and a half million. It's also the centre of Australian jazz. It's been disputed at times, but it always comes back that most of the jazz is occurring in Melbourne. One of the main reasons for this is because of a jazz band called Graham Bell. Graham Bell is fairly well known in America with some of the older collectors, but not with the newer ones. He was a piano player, and with his brother Roger, who is a trumpet player, they started collecting records in the end of the 30s, about 38 or 39, and they started trying to play some jazz, and fairly successfully. And under the influence of Lou Waters mainly, plus the usual Louis Armstrong and Jolly Roll Morton, they made a few records. And at this time, during the war, Max Kaminsky visited Australia, and they got to play with him. In fact, they made a record with him. Unfortunately, I haven't got this record with me. But to give you some idea of the music they played, this is a later record. We will play... Something I don't like doing is playing whatever one considers everyone... Every jazz band should play, and that's tunes like Just a Closer Walk With E. But you'll have to bear with me in this case, because it's the only record of this type I've got. It will also illustrate something that occurs in Australian jazz, and that is that lots of the earlier bands used to have clarinet choruses with two clarinets, and this illustrates just that.

Let me ask you one thing before we get to the recording itself. Graham Bell is from Melbourne, is that correct? That's correct, yeah. And that was his base of activities when he was active back in the 30s and 40s.
Well, he wasn't really active in the 30s. Around about 1938 he tried to play jazz fairly successfully.
When did he form his first band, do you know that?
Around about that time.
About 1938? Yeah. And he was influenced, you say, by Lou Waters, but Lou Waters...
Later. Yeah, recording until the 40s.
How about his early recordings? Well... What did he influence then?
I would say just the normal Armstrong-Oliver records.
Armstrong-Oliver and the small band recordings, Benny Goodman Trio and things of that nature.
I don't know about Benny Goodman, no.
No?
I would say not. More traditional. Yeah.
Strictly traditional, I see. All right. And you say that Melbourne is the center of jazz in Australia. That's right, yeah. How about Sydney? Is there any activity there?
There's quite a lot there. Possibly, there's always been a nucleus of people following traditional jazz, but they're more inclined to modern jazz.
I see. I see. Is there a lot of rivalry between, say, Sydney and Melbourne in the traditional jazz camp?
Not really, no.
Not like, say, for example, in this country between Los Angeles and San Francisco, where they have traditional jazz bands and rivalry between the cities and so on?

Oh, there's a lot of people. There's a lot of rivalry. But it doesn't matter very much. Later on, I'll tell you about our annual jazz convention and just how this would sort of not stop any rivalry, make everyone good friends. Amazing.
Could you give us the personnel of this early recording and perhaps maybe when it was recorded?

Generally, it was a pretty stable group over quite a long time. And as I said, Roger Bell was on trumpet. And the person you'll hear of all through this session is Ade Monsborough, who probably is Australia's best known musician. And he plays a great range of instruments. And on this record, he plays valve trombone and clarinet. Don Pixie Roberts is on clarinet. Graham Bell piano. Bud Baker banjo and guitar. And Lucille Berison on tuba. And Russ Murphy on drums. It was recorded in Melbourne on the 6th of August, 1949.

We have with us tonight, in case you joined us a little bit late, Mr. Eric Brown as our guest commentator this evening, and he is filling us in on the details of these recordings, telling us a little bit about Australian jazz. Eric, what's the story on the next recording?

Well, I'll just give a bit of information on the Graham Bell Band itself. It more or less became very popular just after the war in 1946, and it went to Czechoslovakia to represent Australia at a youth festival. That was in August of 1947. Just before they went, they made a number of 78s. And one of these particular records, Smokey Mokes, got on our hit parade, which was quite an amazing occurrence for that time. When they were at this festival, they were not very enchanted with the festival, so they left and they toured Europe and particularly England. Now, England at that time, there weren't any jazz clubs for dancing, as opposed to jazz clubs for listening. And they more or less introduced jazz clubs to England. And through their inspiration, bands like Humphrey Littleton and various other bands started playing at jazz clubs, and the popularity of jazz in England increased. They then returned home and again toured England in 1950. Then they came back again and were thoroughly sick of playing with each other. And at that time, they made a record, or a number of records, one of which is this one, Sob and Blues, and this was more or less the final form of the band before they broke up. This was recorded in... Well, it was recorded before they went away, but it's more or less the same band as when it came back. They had two trumpets, Roger Bell and now the Aide Monsborough again on trumpet, Pixie Roberts clarinet, Johnny Rich on trombone, Graham Bell piano, Bud Baker banjo, Lou Sobrys and bass, and Jack Banston on drums. And this was recorded in 1949. Southern Blues. Another group that was going at that time was the Southern Jazz Group, who come from Adelaide, which is another capital city of South Australia, which is down next to Victoria, the state in which Melbourne is in. Now, they had a very fine band, and the leader of the band, Dave Dalwitz, was also a composer and composed lots of tunes. And the first one of these we're going to hear is called Emu Strut. This was recorded in 1st of June, 1950. And the members of the band were Bill Munro on trumpet, dug up Ade Monsborough again on trumpet, clarinet, and alto. Bruce Gray, a very fine clarinet player. Dave Dalwitz on trombone. Kevin Allen on piano. Johnny Malpaz on banjo. Bob Wright on tuba. And Bob Foreman on drums.
May I ask you, what is an emu?
An emu is a bird very similar to an ostrich, which is a bird which is only found in Australia.

We're listening to Australian jazz recordings with our guest commentator, Mr. Eric Brown, who is filling us in on some of the details on some of these recordings, personnel, and other interesting facts. The program is Speakeasy Junction. This is Ron Warren, your host, and this is a program that comes to you every Sunday night over at WXFM. We are here from 10 until 1, Monday morning, playing some of the finest in Dixieland, traditional jazz, old recordings from the 1920s, 30s, and 40s, a few comedy records, and we do play requests. If there's anything you would like to hear played on this program, all you have to do is drop me a card or letter and let me know what you want played, and we'll see if the recording is available. We can get it into the program. We had a very nice letter from Mr. Charles Giori, who lives in Glenview, Illinois. He said that he wanted to hear a couple of recordings played possibly before 11 p.m. on this program tonight. Well, unfortunately, we have the special program. It's going to carry on right up until 12 midnight this evening, so if Mr. Giori will bear with us, we will get his recordings on sometime after 12 p.m. He wanted to hear Fats Waller composition and Meadlux Lewis on this program, and we will be playing his requests later on after the special program dedicated to Australian jazz. And that's what we are doing right now over WXFM in Elmwood Park, serving the Chicago area from Studios in Elmwood Park and from Studios High atop, 333 North Michigan, downtown Chicago, 106 on your FM dial. Now we are going to go back to Mr. Brown and have him tell us a little more about the next recording.

Well, we continue on with the Southern Jazz Group, and near the end of their career in 1951, they put out an album of original compositions by Australian jazzmen. In fact, the Australian Broadcasting Commission did a series of programs featuring these compositions, and I think there were 45 in all that they played. And these are some from those particular sessions. Australian jazzmen seem to like to feature funny names of their titles, as you'll see as we go on. And they've got titles on this record like That Imbow Thing, Captivation, Royal Terminus Rag, Shabby Gull Rag, Turquoise Twilight, and this one you're going to hear, which is a Dave Dalwitz composition again, Crocodile Creep. The personnel has changed slightly, and Dave Dalwitz is now playing piano, Keith Hounslow trumpet, Taz Brown clarinet, Mel Wilkinson trombone, Ron Carson banjo, Gubby Allen tuba, and Brian Wright on drums. This was recorded on the 19th of June, 1951. Crocodile Creep. Eric, would you tell us a little bit about Frank Johnson?

Before I do, these two bands, the Southern Jazz Group and Graham Bell's band, plus Tony Newstead, an Eddie Condon type band and another band from Hobart, which is an island below Melbourne, came together just for a holiday, just for fun, and they hired a hall and they all played, just for their own amusement for the whole of the holidays which occurs at Christmas time in Melbourne, and they, as the thing progressed, they charged admission, and then the following year they did it again, and out of that grew what is known as the Australian Jazz Convention, and it's been running every year since 1946, where all the bands from all over Australia congregate in a particular city, and just get together for their own amusement and play the jazz they like, and mix it up and have sitting groups, and through that many musicians have been discovered, and many musicians get their start this way. Also, all the record collectors and the musicians get to know each other.
So the public is invited to these affairs?

They have public concerts during the day. It starts at 10 in the morning and ends at about 11 at night, and that's public concerts, and after that there are after-hours functions, which are closed to the general public, and only musicians and collectors and that can go. And the first night is a sort of a welcoming night, which is known as the how you've been keeping night, which has got free beer and all that sort of thing. That's why the general public is kept out. One day they have a riverboat trip. Some of our rivers have got small, not riverboats by American standards, but enough to take a band and a number of people, and they go up the river and back. They have a final concert where all the best bands of the convention are featured, and they also have a general meeting where everybody goes along and votes which city should have the convention the following year. And when that has been decided, a committee from that particular city is formed, and they work all year to make the convention a success. And any money made from the convention goes on to the following convention.
Do you always play in the larger cities, or have you had any conventions?
Well, we have played in smaller country towns, and very small towns of probably, say, 10,000 people. And they're usually the best ones because everyone lives in close proximity to each other.
How many people usually attend one of these affairs? How many musicians?

Well, the last one was a little bit smaller than usual, but they had 300 musicians coming, which formed 40 bands. Forty bands? Admittedly, some of the musicians played in several bands, but there were 40 bands. All different styles, not of one particular style. You might get a Louis Russell band, or a Lou Waters type of band, or a Eddie Condon type of band. There are all sorts. No special emphasis is given to any particular style. I can see that many people congregating in a small town could create problems. Has it ever? Yes. So many people were accommodated in one country town that they drank the hotel dry and they ran out of beer. So everyone has quite a good time. Now, through these conventions, younger bands started playing, and one of the best of these, and probably one of the best of the Australian bands, again following the Graham Bell tradition, was the Frank Johnson band. And this particular version of the Frank Johnson band was a two trumpet one featuring Frank Johnson on trumpet and Ken Evans on trumpet. Warwick Dyer on trombone, Jeff Kitchen, probably one of our finest ever clarinet players, Jeff Bland piano, Bill Tote banjo, Jack Connolly tuba, and Wes Brown on drums. This was recorded on the 6th of December, 1949. Frank Johnson.
